blocks.x: There was a time when plenty of filmmakers competed to create other cities’ versions of a New York-set Woody Allen dramedy: Relationship-based movies that were rueful, witty, and a little self-aggrandizing, evincing a complicated love for the city at hand. Allen’s fellow stand-up-turned-writer-director Chris Rock, never one to roll with perceived cancellations, keeps the faith in this lineage with Misty Green, a Los Angeles character study replete with walk-and-talks, dinner banter, an impressively starry cast, and a multifaceted female lead. That is to say, it lands somewhere between Deconstructing Harry and Blue Jasmine. Depending on one’s feelings for Allen’s work in 2026, that might in turn sound like an experience that lands somewhere between ambitious and unbearable.

There won’t be as much disagreement, however, about Misty Green herself. Rosalind Eleazar, perhaps best known for TV’s Slow Horses, gives a hypnotic central performance as an actress who has found some success in film and television, winning a supporting-actress Emmy some years ago, only to fall on harder times. The movie begins by giving her a strict deadline: She has one week to vacate her luxe apartment, because it’s not actually hers. The true owner is an aggrieved woman whose husband Misty had been sleeping with—until he died. Unfortunately for Misty, she did not get his agreement to give her the apartment in writing, and her best friend and fellow actress (Anna Kendrick) isn’t in the position to help her out with a place to stay.

As her agent (Topher Grace) points out, some of Misty’s problems can be attributed to the institutional sexism and racism that permeates Hollywood. He goes on, however, to say that those conditions alone cannot account for her stalled career. That can be attributed to additional factors, such as stubbornness, defiance, and cocaine, which tends to boost those former two. The movie mostly takes place over Misty’s final week in her apartment, and in that timeframe it’s difficult to tell whether she is a proper addict, simply open to a variety of methods for numbing her pain, or if difference ultimately matters, especially to her. Eleazar, with her powerfully hard stare and occasional moments of unguarded charm, makes Misty a genuinely fascinating, knotty subject regardless of her motivations. She’s also able to summon Misty’s obvious talent at will, delineating clear differences between a half-assed audition and one where she’s bringing the electricity that almost made her a star without obviously altering her volume. (She saves that for when the audition is interrupted; Misty is constitutionally incapable of taking setbacks with gentle good humor.)

Eleazar is supported by the kind of rep company—Kendrick, Grace, Daniel Kaluuya, Adam Driver, Alexandra Shipp—that erroneously suggests Rock has spent the 12 years since his also-star-studded Top Five making increasingly acclaimed films, rather than doing cameos, rebooting Saw, and braving the consequences of belated G.I. Jane jokes. She’s less supported by Rock himself, who steps in front of the camera to play Jordan Green, a movie director who shares a name with Misty’s bipolar brother (Kaluuya, typically stellar in an underwritten role). Jordan crossed paths with Misty early in her career, and is now working on another remake of Dreamgirls for which Misty, who sings at a hotel bar on the side, would be perfect.

Jordan and Misty also seem attracted to each other, though he diagnoses Misty as “always acting.” That certainly seems to be how and why she keeps circling back to Zach (Driver), a lower-rent (and coke-loving) filmmaker who has a line on some quick cash if Misty is willing to take a little jaunt to Dubai for an overnight visit with a shady prince. After introducing multiple story threads with compelling scenes placing Eleazar opposite Kendrick, Kaluuya, and a number of wary casting directors, Rock seems to settle on pitting his character against Driver for sort of an unofficial tug-of-war over Misty’s soul.

This is not one of those love triangles where both men turn out to be equally toxic in their own way. Rock keeps carving out time for himself to do admittedly funny but out-of-place bits—returning to Woody Allen, picture him doing one-liners in the middle of Blue Jasmine—which turns out to be preferable to his semi-terrible acting, where he must project stern disapproval of Misty’s antics, often while wearing a stupid hat. In the final stretch, the movie seems rigged to push Misty toward ever-worse decisions as Rock the director all but leers at the tragic but vaguely lascivious results, like he’s spent a bit too much time rewatching Requiem For A Dream. The movie calms down for a lower-key final scene, but it still somehow places Rock’s character back at the center of the narrative. How much can anyone be expected to care about the incoherent arc of Jordan Green’s directorial career?

Misty, though, is nearly compelling enough on her own to justify the time spent with far more sketchily defined characters. Through whatever combination of Eleazar’s acting and Rock’s writing—he must be giving her something to work with, even if it’s wounded by self-regard—Misty Green lives and breathes in a way that Misty Green doesn’t.
Starring: Rosalind Eleazar, Chris Rock, Anna Kendrick, Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Topher Grace
